opus-5.5.text:
I think the most interesting part is that, for a model company, the agent product isn't really a separate thing from the model. It's more like the model's natural body. When you build the product yourself, you see very directly where the model fails: where it loses track over a long task, where tool use breaks, where it's overconfident. That feedback goes straight back into training. So the product becomes part of the research loop, not just a way to distribute the model.

In the earlier chatbot phase, the interaction was mostly one turn or a few turns, and the value was in the answer. With agents, the value is in finishing a task: searching, reading, writing code, running it, correcting itself, maybe over dozens or hundreds of steps. That's a very different capability, and it's hard to optimize if you only see the model from the outside through an API. You need to own the whole environment, the tools, the context management, how the trajectory is evaluated. Doing first-party agents forces you to understand all of that.

There's also a deeper point. I've always believed that the ceiling of the model is what matters most, and the product should be designed so it grows with the model. If you put too much hand-crafted workflow around a weak model, you get something that works today, but when the next model comes out, a lot of that scaffolding becomes a burden. Model companies are in a good position to make the opposite bet: keep the product structure simple and general, and let the model's improvement show up directly as product improvement.

And finally, agents change what "data" means. In the past, a lot of the progress came from static internet data. Now a lot of it can come from interaction: the model acting in an environment and getting a signal about whether it succeeded. A first-party agent product is one of the best ways to discover what tasks really matter to people and what a good outcome looks like. In that sense, the product helps define the next training objective. I find that loop, product to model and model back to product, the most exciting part.

r001.rationale: The response says that too much hand-crafted workflow around a weak model can become a burden, but it does not characterize earlier agent products as having been built that way.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the interesting thing is that it changes the relationship between the model and the product. For a long time, the assumption was that a model company builds the base model, exposes an API, and then other people figure out what to do with it. The agent layer was supposed to be someone else's job. But what we're seeing now is that the agent is not really a thin wrapper anymore. The way you do planning, tool use, memory, how you recover from errors, how you decide when to stop and ask the user, all of that depends very heavily on how the model was trained. So if you want the agent to be good, you almost have to train the model with that agent in mind. The product and the model become one system.

That is also why I think first-party agents are a kind of data strategy, not just a revenue strategy. When you own the product, you see the whole trajectory, not just a single prompt and response. You see where the agent got stuck, where the user intervened, which tasks took thirty steps when they should have taken five. That is exactly the signal you need for reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks, and it is very hard to get that signal through an API where you only see fragments.

The other thing I find interesting is that it forces the model company to confront what the model actually cannot do. When you're only shipping a model, it's easy to point at benchmarks and say it's strong. When you have to ship a coding agent or a research agent that people use every day, you discover that the bottleneck is often not raw intelligence but things like reliability over many steps, knowing what it doesn't know, or managing context over hours of work. Those are the problems that matter now, and I think building the product is the fastest way to find them. So for me the question is not really whether model companies should build agents, it is whether you can be a serious model company in this phase without doing it.

r001.rationale: The response says the prior assumption was to expose a base model through an API and leave the agent layer to others, then describes the agent as no longer being a “thin wrapper.” This conveys earlier agents as wrappers built around a foundation model.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting part is the feedback loop between the model and the product. When you build an agent, you start to see capabilities that are hard to measure just by looking at individual model responses. Can it carry out a longer task? Can it recognize when something went wrong and recover? Does it know when to ask the user for more information?

If you build both the model and the product, those observations can inform what you train for next. And as the model improves, you can rethink the product experience. So the two can evolve together.

But owning the model doesn’t automatically mean you’ll build the best product. You still have to understand what users actually want to delegate and make the agent reliable enough that delegating saves them work. To me, that’s the interesting question: how much advantage can you get from making those model and product decisions together?

r001.rationale: The response discusses building an agent and the model–product feedback loop, but does not characterize earlier agent products as scaffolding added around a foundation model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s interesting is that the model and the product start to shape each other much more directly. With an agent, you’re not just asking whether the model gives a good answer. You’re asking whether it can finish a task, use tools, recover from mistakes, and know when it needs more information. Building the product yourself gives you a much clearer view of where the model is actually falling short.

That creates a useful feedback loop. You can improve the model, but you can also change the tools, the interface, or the way the task is structured. Sometimes what looks like a model limitation is really a product problem, and sometimes the product can’t improve until the model gets better.

The tension is that a model company also wants to serve developers building their own products. So I think the interesting question is how you use first-party products to push the technology forward while still making the underlying platform valuable to everyone else.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how first-party agent products connect with model development, tools, and interfaces, but does not describe earlier agent products as scaffolding built around a foundation model.
